questions.question: A 35-year-old athlete presents with difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a seated position. Upon examination, there is weakness in hip extension. Which muscle is most likely affected, and what is the nerve supply?

options.A: Psoas major; Anterior rami of L1, L2, L3

explanation.text: Gluteus maximus is the chief extensor of the hip, and weakness would impair actions like rising from a seated position. Its nerve supply is the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).

Action of the Hip joint, corresponding muscles and their innervation: Action Muscles Nerve supply Flexion Psoas major (chief flexor) (Option A) Anterior rami of L1, L2, L3 Iliacus (chief flexor) Sartorius (Option D) Rectus femoris Pectineus Femoral nerve (L2, L3) Extension Gluteus maximus (chief extensor) (Option B) Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) Hamstring muscles Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2) Abduction Gluteus medius and minimus (chief abductors) Tensor fasciae latae Superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1) (Option C) Adduction Adductor longus Adductor brevis Adductor magnus (chief adductors) Gracilis Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) Pectineus Double nerve supply (Femoral nerve and obturator nerve) Medial rotation Anterior fibres of gluteus minimus and medius (chief medial rotators) Tensor fasciae latae Superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1) Lateral rotation Piriformis Ventral rami of S1, S2 Obturator externus Posterior division of obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) Obturator internus and Associated gemelli, Quadratus femoris (These muscles are generally termed short rotators) Nerve to obturator internus (L5, S1, S2)

questions.question: In a clinical setting, a physician suspects a weakness in the gluteus maximus muscle. Which of the following functions would not be affected by this?

options.C: Lateral rotation and abduction of the thigh
options.D: Stabilization of pelvis during quiet standing

explanation.text: The gluteus maximus muscle stabilizes the hip during walking and not during quiet standing. It is one of the major muscles of the gluteal region.

Features Largest and most superficial in the gluteal region Broad, thick, and quadrilateral Has an overlying adipose fascia Fascicular architecture with large bundles of fibres separated by fibrous septa Origin Gluteal surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line Outer slope of the dorsal segment of ilium Dorsal surfaces of the sacrum and ilium Sacrotuberous ligament Insertions 3/4th of the muscle into the iliotibial tract 1/4th of the muscle into the gluteal tuberosity Vascular Supply Primarily supplied by the inferior gluteal artery (≈ 2/3) Superior gluteal artery Additional supply from the first perforator of profunda femoris and medial circumflex femoral artery Minor branches from lateral circumflex femoral, lateral sacral, and internal pudendal arteries.

**Innervation Innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) Actions Extends flexed thigh (Option A):** Stabilizes pelvis during gait (vs Option D) Active in raising trunk after stooping (Option B) Active in lateral rotation and abduction of the thigh (Option C) Stabilizes femur via iliotibial tract The gluteus maximus is generally inactive during Quiet standing When swaying forward at the ankle joints When bending forward at the hip joints to touch the toes Testing Tested by hip extension against resistance in prone position with knees flexed

questions.question: A 30-year-old runner complains of difficulty flexing his knee after long-distance running. He reports that once his knee locks in an extended position, it takes effort to initiate flexion again. On examination, you notice that the patient struggles to begin flexion from full extension. Which muscle is likely impaired?

explanation.text: The popliteus muscle is responsible for unlocking the knee by causing lateral rotation of the femur on the tibia during the initial phase of flexion. Impairment of this muscle would make it difficult to initiate flexion from full extension.

Action of the knee joint, corresponding muscles and their innervation Action Muscle Innervation Flexion Biceps femoris Semitendinosus Semimembranosus Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2) Extension Quadriceps femoris (Option A) Femoral nerve Medial rotation of flexed leg Popliteus Tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1) Semimembranosus Semitendinosus Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2) Lateral rotation of flexed leg Biceps femoris (Option C) Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2) Locking Vastus medialis (Option D) Femoral nerve Unlocking Popliteus (Option B) Tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1) Locking Unlocking Medial rotation of the femur on the tibia during the terminal phase of extension.

Lateral rotation of the femur on the tibia during the initial phase of the flexion It is brought about by the quadriceps femoris It is brought about by the popliteus muscle Locked knee becomes rigid Unlocked knee can be further flexed All ligaments are taut All ligaments are relaxed Pathological locking A meniscus tear can cause a knee to lock when a torn piece of cartilage falls off and gets stuck in the knee, or when a large tear folds over and gets stuck.
This is called true locking. Pseudo locking is when the knee can't fully extend due to pain or an effusion.

questions.question: The iliotibial tract provides attachment to which of the following muscles?

explanation.text: The deep fascia of the thigh presents two modifications – iliotibial tract and saphenous opening. Iliotibial tract: The iliotibial tract splits into two layers to enclose the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus

muscles. Between these muscles, it forms a thickened sheet called the gluteal aponeurosis, which also covers the gluteus medius. The superficial lamina attaches to the tubercle of the iliac crest. The deep lamina attaches to the capsule of the hip joint. Inferiorly, the tract attaches to a smooth area on the anterior surface of the lateral condyle of the tibia. Function: Stabilizes the knee both in extension and in partial flexion.
Used during walking and running. When leaning forward with slightly flexed knees, the iliotibial tract supports the knee against gravity, preventing the individual from falling forward.

questions.question: Which of the following does not participate in the cruciate anastomosis?

explanation.text: Cruciate anastomosis is situated at the upper part of the back of the femur at the level of lesser trochanter. The cruciate anastomosis is formed by the following arteries: Transverse branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery. Transverse branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery. Ascending branch of the first perforating artery. Descending branch of the inferior gluteal artery.

questions.question: The femoral nerve splits into anterior and posterior divisions, which are separated by which of the following structures?

explanation.text: The chief nerve of the anterior compartment of the thigh is the femoral nerve. It is the largest branch of the lumbar plexus and arises from the dorsal divisions of the anterior primary rami of the L2, L3, and L4 nerves. The femoral nerve enters the thigh posterior to the inguinal ligament, just lateral to the femoral sheath.
About 2 cm below the inguinal ligament, the femoral nerve divides into anterior and posterior divisions, separated by the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

Anterior Division: Gives off two cutaneous branches and one muscular branch: Medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh (cutaneous) Intermediate cutaneous nerve of the thigh (cutaneous) Muscular branch to the sartorius muscle Posterior Division: Gives off one cutaneous branch and four muscular branches: Saphenous nerve (cutaneous) Muscular branches supplying the quadriceps femoris.

options.C: Medial Pectoral Nerve and Lateral Pectoral Nerve

explanation.text: The Pectenius muscle is a composite/hybrid muscle that is innervated by both the obturator and femoral nerve. Hybrid muscles Composite or hybrid muscles contain multiple fiber types that perform the same function and are innervated by different nerves for each fiber set.

options.A: Nerve to obturator internus passes above it
options.B: Innervated by L5, S1 nerve roots
options.D: It is a medial rotator of the hip joint

explanation.text: The structure marked here is the Piriformis muscle, and the Pudendal nerve passes inferior to it. Piriformis: Attachments Origin: Anterior surface of sacrum (3 digitations) Gluteal surface of ilium near posterior inferior iliac spine Capsule of sacroiliac joint Insertion: Medial side of the upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur The piriformis muscle emerges from the pelvis, almost filling the greater sciatic foramen completely and
is the key muscle of the area.

**Structures running superior to piriformis Superior gluteal nerve and vessel (Option A):** Structures running inferior to piriformis. Inferior gluteal nerve and vessels Greater trochanter Sciatic nerve Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh Nerve to quadratus femoris Nerve to obturator internus Internal pudendal vessels Pudendal nerve (Option C) Vascular Supply Main supply: Superior gluteal artery Contributions: Gemellar branches of internal pudendal, inferior gluteal artery, lateral sacral artery Innervation Innervated by superior gluteal nerve and ventral rami of S1 and S2 (Option B) Actions Laterally rotates extended thigh (Option D) Abducts flexed thigh Testing No isolated testing; assess for dysfunction by having the seated subject abduct thighs (buttock pain indicates potential involvement) Pudendal Nerve: Origin: Arises from the ventral divisions of S2, S3, and S4 sacral ventral rami. Formation Location: Just above the superior border of the sacrotuberous ligament and upper fibres of ischiococcygeus. Leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen between piriformis and ischiococcygeus. Pathway: Enters the gluteal region. Passes dorsal to the sacrospinous ligament, near its attachment to the ischial spine. Lies medially to the internal pudendal vessels. Further Course: Accompanies the internal pudendal artery through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal. Branches: In the posterior part of the canal, gives rise to: Inferior anal nerve Perineal nerve Dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris (continues anteriorly)

questions.question: A 30-year-old male is being examined for abnormal gait. His Trendelenberg sign is positive. What is false about testing for the Trendelenburg sign?

options.A: The side of the hip that droops down is the unaffected side
options.B: The gluteus medius and minimus muscles are affected
options.C: The patients have a characteristic lurching gait
options.D: The uncompensated Trendelenburg sign is elicited with a walking patient

explanation.text: The uncompensated Trendelenburg sign is elicited in a patient in a standing position on one limb and the compensated is elicited in a walking patient. Tensor Fasciae Latae Gluteus Medius Gluteus Minimus Attachments Origin: Outer lip of the iliac crest extending from the anterior superior iliac spine to the tubercle of the crest. Insertion: Iliotibial tract 3–5 cm below the level of the greater trochanter.

Origin: Gluteal surface of the ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines Insertion: Oblique ridge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. Origin: Gluteal surfaces of the ilium between anterior & inferior gluteal lines.

Insertion: Anterior aspect of the Greater trochanter Relations Between gluteus medius and sartorius Covered by fascia lata Covered by gluteus maximus (posterior third) Deep to gluteus minimus Deep to gluteus medius Related to hip joint capsule Vascular Supply Mainly from lateral circumflex femoral artery Supplied by superior gluteal artery Deep branch of superior gluteal artery Trochanteric anastomosis Main trunk and deep branch of superior gluteal arter y Trochanteric anastomosis Innervation Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) Actions Hip flexor and abductor Stabilizes pelvis Helps maintain extended knee Abducts thigh Medial & lateral rotation of thigh Supports pelvis during single-leg stance Abducts thigh Medial and lateral rotation of thigh Testing Depression below anterior superior iliac spine Abduction against resistance Medial rotation against resistance Abduction against resistance Medial rotation against resistance Abduction against resistance Trendelenberg sign: When the body's weight is balanced on one leg, the gluteal muscles on the supported side help elevate the opposite, unsupported side of the pelvis.
**However, if there is a malfunction in the abductor mechanism, the Sound side sinks (Option A):** which is referred to as a positive Trendelenburg sign (uncompensated).

**This sign indicates issues with hip abductors, such as paralysis of the gluteus medius and minimus (Option B):** ; problems with the fulcrum, including congenital or pathological hip dislocations; and concerns related to body weight, such as an unhealed fracture of the femoral neck. When patients with the gluteus medius and minimus paralysis walk, they have a characteristic lurching gait (Option C) ie, during the single leg supporting phase of walking, there is leaning of the trunk to the affected side known as the compensated Trendelenburg sign. Duck waddling gait is seen when both the sides are affected.

questions.question: A patient reports pain and decreased sensation along the posterolateral aspect of the lower leg, extending onto the lateral side of the foot, following an ankle sprain. Which nerve is most likely injured?

explanation.text: The sural nerve innervates the posterolateral aspect of the leg. Injury can occur due to ankle sprains, fractures, or tight footwear, leading to pain and sensory loss in this region. Cutaneous Innervation of Lower Limb: Primarily from the lumbar and sacral plexuses. Except some proximal uni segmental nerves arise from T12 or L1 spinal nerves.

Thigh Innervation: Main supply: Lateral and Posterior Cutaneous Nerves of the Thigh and Cutaneous Branch of Femoral Nerve. Leg Innervation: Anteromedial Aspect: Saphenous nerve (Option B) Posterolateral Aspect: Sural nerve Anterolateral Aspect: Superficial peroneal nerve (Option C) Foot Innervation: Dorsum of the Foot: Mainly by superficial peroneal nerves. Sole of the Foot: Supplied by cutaneous branches of medial and lateral plantar nerves.

Nerve Injury Risks: Iliohypogastric, Ilioinguinal, and Genitofemoral Nerve Injury: Common during lower abdomen or spine surgeries. Can result in anesthesia, hyperesthesia, neuralgia or causalgia in their sensory distribution. Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Injury: (Option D) Vulnerable to entrapment beneath the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine.

Causes paresthesia or dysaesthesia (meralgia paresthetica) on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh, intensified by walking or hip extension. Sural Nerve Injury: (Option A) Occur at the level of the ankle due to fractures or sprain, tight shoes, or surgery. Cause pain and diminished sensation along the postero-lateral lower leg extending onto the lateral surface of the ankle and foot.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is involved in a car accident and sustains a fracture to the ischial tuberosity. He now presents with weakness in knee flexion and hip extension, with intact sensation. Which muscle group and nerve are likely involved?

explanation.text: The hamstrings, innervated by the sciatic nerve, are responsible for knee flexion and hip extension. A fracture of the ischial tuberosity can affect the attachment site of these muscles. Sciatic nerve Size and Origin: Thickest nerve in the body (1.5 to 2 cm wide). Arises from the sacral plexus in the pelvis. Components: Tibial Part: Formed by ventral divisions of anterior primary rami (L4, L5, S1, S2, S3).

Common Peroneal Part: Formed by dorsal divisions of anterior primary rami (L4, L5, S1, S2). Course: Begins in the pelvis, in front of the piriformis muscle. Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis. Divides into tibial and common peroneal nerves at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa. Relations: Deep Relations: Ischium, tendon of obturator internus, quadratus femoris, adductor magnus.
Superficial Relations: Gluteus maximus (in the gluteal region) and long head of biceps femoris (in the thigh). Branches: Articular branches to the hip joint (gluteal region).

**Muscular branches (Option B):** The tibial part supplies the semitendinosus, the semimembranosus, the long head of the biceps femoris, and the ischial head of the adductor magnus (medial side) The common peroneal part supplies only a short head of biceps femoris (lateral side). Clinical Correlation: Compression against the femur can cause "sleeping foot," resulting in lower limb paresthesia when sitting for long periods.
**Quadriceps; femoral nerve (Option A):** Quadriceps extend the knee, not flex it.
**Adductors; obturator nerve (Option C):** Adductors handle hip adduction, not knee flexion or hip extension.
**Gluteal muscles; superior gluteal nerve (Option D):** Gluteal muscles control hip abduction, not knee flexion or hip extension.

options.A: a) Semitendinosus, b) Biceps femoris, c) Popliteal artery, d) Tibial nerve
options.B: a) Semitendinosus, b) Biceps femoris, c) Tibial nerve, d) Popliteal artery
options.C: a) Biceps femoris, b) Semitendinosus, c) Popliteal artery, d) Tibial nerve
options.D: a) Biceps femoris, b) Semitendinosus, c) Tibial nerve, d) Popliteal artery

explanation.text: The given image is the right popliteal fossa; therefore, The Superolateral boundary is formed by a) Biceps femoris The Superomedial boundary is formed by b) the Semitendinosus Marked structure c) is Tibial nerve and d) is Popliteal artery because in the upper part of the fossa, nerve is lateral and the artery is medial.
Popliteal fossa The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped hollow at the back of the knee, becoming prominent when flexed, and serves as a passage for major vessels and nerves between the thigh and leg.

Boundaries Superomedial: Semitendinosus and Semimembranosus Superolateral: Biceps Femoris Inferomedial: Medial head of Gastrocnemius Inferolateral: Lateral head of Gastrocnemius and Plantaris Floor (anterior wall): Formed by the popliteal surface of the femur, knee joint capsule, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia covering the

popliteus muscle. Roof (posterior wall): Formed by the popliteal fascia, containing the short saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh, sural communicating nerve). All structures pierce the roof except the medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

Contents Main Contents: Popliteal artery and branches Popliteal vein and tributaries Tibial nerve and branches Common peroneal nerve and branches Popliteal lymph nodes Popliteal fat pad Additional Structures: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh (terminal part) Descending genicular branch of obturator nerve Terminal part of the short saphenous vein Arrangement of Key Structures (NVA/AVN pattern) Upper part: Nerve, Vein, Artery (lateral to medial) Middle part: Nerve, Vein, Artery (superficial to deep) Lower part: Artery, Vein, Nerve (lateral to medial)

questions.question: Which of the following sets of muscles is referred to as "guy rope" muscles that stabilise the bony pelvis on the femur?

explanation.text: The term "guy rope muscles" refers to the Sartorius, Gracilis, and Semitendinosus muscles, which each originate from different compartments of the thigh—anterior, medial, and posterior, respectively. These
muscles play a crucial role in stabilizing the pelvis on the femur. Guy rope muscles 1. Sartorius 2. Gracilis 3.

Semitendinosus Compartment Part of the anterior compartment Part of the medial compartment Part of the posterior compartment Innervation Femoral nerve Obturator nerve Sciatic nerve Action Hip flexion, abduction, and external rotation Hip adduction and knee flexion Knee flexion and hip extension Origin Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) Inferior pubic ramus Ischial tuberosity Insertion Upper part of the medial surface of the tibia. (Pes anserinus or Goosefoot tendon is the broad, conjoined tendon formed by these 3 muscles, inserting on the medial surface of the proximal tibia) Together, these muscles anchor below at the tibia, spreading out above to support the pelvic structure, functioning effectively like "guy ropes" to maintain stability.

Bursa Anserinus, situated on the upper medial surface of the tibia, separates the tendons of the Sartorius, Gracilis, and Semitendinosus muscles at their insertion points and also isolates them from the tibial collateral ligament.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male presents with difficulty in adducting his thigh after sustaining an injury during a soccer match. Upon examination, weakness in adduction and medial rotation of the thigh is noted. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for these actions, and what is its nerve supply?

options.D: Adductor part of adductor magnus; Obturator nerve (posterior division)

explanation.text: The adductor part of the adductor magnus muscle is primarily responsible for thigh adduction and medial rotation. It is innervated by the obturator nerve, specifically the posterior division. The weakness observed in these actions following the injury indicates the involvement of adductor magnus.

Neurological examination reveals weakness in plantar flexion, inability to flex his toes and diminished ankle reflexes. Which spinal cord segments are primarily involved in this patient's symptoms?

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with a foot drop following a recent knee injury. Which of the following nerves, part of the sacral plexus, is most likely injured, leading to the inability to dorsiflex the foot?

explanation.text: Common peroneal nerve branches from the sciatic nerve and innervates the muscles responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot (e.g., tibialis anterior is supplied by deep peroneal nerve, which is a branch of common peroneal nerve). Injury to this nerve often results in foot drop.

Sacral Plexus: The sacral plexus is a complex network of nerves formed by the anterior rami (ventral rami) of the L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3 spinal nerves, with some contributions from S4. It is located on the posterior wall of the pelvis, resting on the anterior surface of the piriformis muscle. The sacral plexus plays a critical role in providing motor and sensory innervation to parts of the pelvis, perineum, and lower limbs.

Root Values and Divisions Root Values: L4 to S4 contribute to the sacral plexus. Divisions: Anterior Division: Primarily supplies muscles involved in flexion and related functions. Posterior Division: Supplies muscles associated with extension and related movements. Major Nerves of the Sacral Plexus Nerve Formation Pathway Functions Sciatic Nerve The largest nerve in the body, derived from both

anterior and posterior divisions of L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3. Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, passing beneath the piriformis muscle, and travels down the posterior thigh. Supplies the posterior thigh muscles. It divides into two key branches: Tibial Nerve (Anterior Division) (Option B): Innervates the posterior leg and foot muscles. Common Peroneal Nerve (Posterior Division): Innervates muscles of the lateral and anterior leg.
Clinical Note: Injury to the common peroneal nerve can result in foot drop, a condition characterized by difficulty lifting the front part of the foot.

**Pudendal Nerve (Option D):** Arises from the anterior divisions of S2, S3, and S4. Travels out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and into the perineum via the lesser sciatic foramen. Provides motor and sensory innervation to the perineum, including muscles of the pelvic floor and external genitalia. It is crucial for maintaining continence and sexual function. Superior Gluteal Nerve Originates from the posterior divisions of L4, L5, and S1. Exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen, superior to the piriformis muscle. Innervates the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae, which are responsible for hip abduction and pelvis stabilization during walking. Inferior Gluteal Nerve Originates from the posterior divisions of L5, S1, and S2. Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, inferior to the piriformis. Innervates the gluteus maximus, the primary extensor of the hip joint.

**Posterior Femoral Cutaneous Nerve (Option A):** Arises from the anterior and posterior divisions of S1, S2, and S3. Travels alongside the sciatic nerve, exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. Provides sensory innervation to the skin on the posterior thigh and lower buttocks. Minor Nerves of the Sacral Plexus Nerve to Piriformis (S1, S2): Supplies the piriformis muscle, which assists in lateral rotation of the hip. Nerve to Quadratus Femoris (L4, L5, S1): Innervates the quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus muscles, responsible for lateral hip rotation and stabilization. Nerve to Obturator Internus (L5, S1, S2): Innervates the obturator internus and superior gemellus muscles, involved in lateral rotation of the thigh. Lumbosacral Trunk The lumbosacral trunk, formed by the anterior rami of L4 and L5, contributes to the sacral plexus and joins the sacral nerves to form branches that innervate the lower extremities. Clinical Relevance Sciatica: Compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve leads to pain that radiates down the leg (sciatica). Pudendal Neuralgia: Compression of the pudendal nerve can cause pain or dysfunction in the perineal region, impacting bladder control, bowel function, and sexual health. Piriformis Syndrome: In certain individuals, the sciatic nerve may pass through the piriformis muscle, leading to entrapment and pain. Foot Drop: Injury to the common peroneal nerve can cause foot drop, where a person cannot dorsiflex the foot, leading to a characteristic "slapping" gait.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of tingling and numbness in the outer aspect of his right thigh. He reports that the symptoms worsen when he sits for prolonged periods and improves when he stands or walks. Upon examination, there is a sensory deficit in the lateral thigh region. Which nerve root value is primarily involved in this condition?

explanation.text: Based on the clinical scenario, the patient's symptoms align with meralgia paresthetica, marked by tingling and numbness in the outer thigh that worsens with prolonged sitting and improves with standing or walking. This condition results from compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, which is primarily derived from the dorsal divisions of the L2 and L3 nerve roots.

Lumbar Plexus: The lumbar plexus is a network of nerves formed by the anterior rami (ventral rami) of the lumbar spinal nerves, specifically L1 to L4. It is located within the psoas major muscle in the posterior abdominal wall. The lumbar plexus is responsible for providing motor and sensory innervation to the pelvic region and the lower limb.

Division of Roots The roots of the lumbar plexus can be categorised into two main divisions: Anterior Division: Comprising roots that generally supply flexor muscles and associated sensory areas. Posterior Division: Comprising roots that typically supply extensor muscles and their corresponding sensory territories.

Major Nerves of the Lumbar Plexus Nerve Formation Pathway Functions Obturator Nerve Formed from the ventral divisions of L2, L3, and L4. It exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen. Innervates the muscles of the medial thigh (adductors) and provides sensory innervation to the skin of the medial thigh.

Femoral Nerve Formed from the dorsal divisions of L2, L3, and L4. (Option C) It passes under the inguinal ligament into the anterior compartment of the thigh. Supplies the muscles of the anterior thigh (such as quadriceps) and provides sensory innervation to the anterior thigh and part of the medial leg. Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve Formed from the dorsal divisions of L2 and L3.

It courses laterally across the iliacus muscle and under the inguinal ligament. Provides purely sensory innervation to the skin over the lateral aspect of the thigh. This nerve is particularly important in conditions such as meralgia paresthetica, where it can become compressed, leading to tingling and pain in the outer thigh. Most commonly injured during Mc Roberts manure & Laproscopic hernia surgery.

Proximal Nerves: Iliohypogastric Nerve (L1) Function: Supplies the skin over the lower abdomen and contributes to abdominal muscle innervation. Most common nerve entrapped in open inguinal hernia surgery, leads to the common cause of pain syndrome. Ilioinguinal Nerve (L1) Function: Provides sensory innervation to the skin of the groin, part of the thigh, root of the penis, clitoris, and anterior of the scrotum.

**Genitofemoral Nerve (L1, L2) (Option A):** Branches: Genital Branch: Supplies the cremaster muscle and the skin of the scrotum in males, and the labia majora in females. Efferent for cremasteric reflex. It is injured in open hernia repair. Femoral Branch: Supplies the skin of the upper anterior thigh. Afferent for cremasteric reflex. It is anesthetized in femoral vein catheterization.
**Lumbosacral Trunk (L4, L5) (Option D):** Function: Contributes to the formation of the sacral plexus, which innervates the lower limb.

questions.question: A 28 y/o football player experiences sudden pain on the inside of his left knee after getting tackled while running with the ball. He reports feeling a pop and is unable to continue playing. O/E, there is swelling, tenderness along the medial joint line, and pain when attempting to flex the knee. Which of the following injuries is most likely?

explanation.text: The mechanism of injury (sudden pain on the inside of the knee, feeling a pop, and tenderness along the medial joint line) is characteristic of a medial meniscus tear, which is often associated with twisting movements and trauma.

Football Player Knee Injuries: Structures in the knee and injuries Cruciate Ligaments The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is more vulnerable than the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) due to rotational forces in football. (Options B&D ruled out) Sudden direction changes can overstretch and tear the ACL. Collateral Ligaments (Lateral & medial) Less frequently injured but essential for side-to-side stability. (Option A ruled out) Side tackles (severe adduction or abduction) can strain these structures, leading to tears or sprains.

Menisci Medial Meniscus is more prone to injury than the lateral meniscus. The medial meniscus attaches to the tibial collateral ligament- hence, it is more susceptible to tears from rotational forces. Bucket-handle tears are common in athletes and are characterised by longitudinal meniscus tears due to pivoting and twisting in a slightly flexed knee. Menisci

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding sustentaculum tali is correct. It is a shelf like projection, projecting from posterior surface of calcaneus. Superior surface of sustentaculum tali bears a facet for talus. Inferior surface of sustentaculum tali bears a groove for the tendon of flexor hallucis longus The medial surface of sustentaculum tali provides attachment to spring ligament and superficial fibres of deltoid ligament

explanation.text: Calcaneus: The calcaneus is the largest and strongest bone of the foot. It is situated below the talus and extends behind it. It is directed forward and laterally with an upward inclination. Anterior surface It is the smallest and bears a concavo-convex articular facet to articulate with cuboid. Posterior surface: It is divided into the following three parts: The upper one-third is smooth and related to a synovial bursa.

The middle one-third provides attachment to tendocalcaneus and plantaris. Lower one-third is subcutaneous and weight bearing during standing posture Superior (dorsal) surface: It is divided into the following three areas: Posterior one-third (non-articular). Middle one-third (articular). Anterior one-third (partly articular and partly nonarticular). Plantar (inferior) surface: It is rough and marked by three tubercles.

A small tubercle at the anterior end is called anterior tubercle. An elevation at its posterior end is called calcaneal tuberosity presenting a large medial and small lateral tubercles. The triangular area between the three tubercles provides attachment to the long plantar ligament. A groove in front of the anterior tubercle gives attachment to short plantar ligament Lateral surface It is almost flat and subcutaneous.
It presents a small elevation in its anterior part called peroneal trochlea (tubercle) which lies 2 cm below the tip of lateral malleolus.

Medial surface: It is concave from above downward A shelf-like projection called sustentaculum tali projects from its upper anterior part. (Statement 1) The superior surface of sustentaculum tali bears a facet for talus (Statement 2) while its inferior surface bears a groove for the tendon of flexor hallucis longus. (Statement 3) Tendon of flexor digitorum longus is related to the medial surface of sustentaculum tali.

Medial surface of sustentaculum tali provides attachments to the following structures from anterior to posterior (Statement 4): (a) Spring ligament. (b) A slip from the tibialis posterior tendon. (c) Deltoid ligament (superficial fibres). (d) Medial talocalcaneal ligament. Reference:
